title: Shallow Diagonals of Pascal's Triangle Are Fibonacci
content:
One of the most celebrated hidden patterns in Pascal's triangle: summing the binomial coefficients along a **shallow (rising) diagonal** reproduces the Fibonacci numbers,
$$\sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n-j}{j} = F_{n+1}.$$
The terms $\binom{n}{0}, \binom{n-1}{1}, \binom{n-2}{2}, \dots$ run up a diagonal of slope $2$ and vanish once $2j > n$, so the sum is finite. The parent entry recorded this only as `native_decide`-checked numeric examples and posed the general proof as its first open question; this file discharges it for all $n$, axiom-free, by recognizing the identity already living inside Mathlib's antidiagonal Fibonacci sum.

title: Why Fibonacci Appears: Tilings and Pascal's Rule
content: The proof here is a reindexing of a Mathlib lemma, but the *reason* the diagonal sum is Fibonacci is combinatorial. Count the tilings of a $1 \times n$ strip by unit squares and dominoes: a tiling using $j$ dominoes uses $n - 2j$ squares, hence $n - j$ tiles in total, and choosing which $j$ of those tiles are dominoes gives $\binom{n-j}{j}$ tilings. Summing over $j$ counts *all* tilings, and that count satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence (a strip ends in either a square or a domino), so it equals $F_{n+1}$. The same recurrence appears algebraically through Pascal's rule $\binom{n-j}{j} = \binom{n-1-j}{j} + \binom{n-1-j}{j-1}$, which splits the level-$n$ diagonal sum into the level-$(n-1)$ and level-$(n-2)$ sums — exactly $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. A direct Lean formalization of this bijection is left as one of the entry's open questions.
mathContext: $\#\{\text{square/domino tilings of }1\times n\} = \sum_{j} \binom{n-j}{j} = F_{n+1}$; Pascal's rule reproduces $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$.

title: Automatic Finiteness From Vanishing Binomials
content: Both theorems sum over the full `Finset.range (n + 1)`, yet the shallow diagonal only has $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ nonzero terms. No explicit truncation is needed: `Nat.choose (n - j) j` is definitionally $0$ as soon as the lower index exceeds the upper, i.e. once $2j > n$. Summing over the convenient bound $j \le n$ therefore introduces only honest zeros and keeps the index algebra clean — this is what lets the antidiagonal sum and the reflected range sum line up term-for-term without case splits. Working over `range (n + 1)` rather than `range (n/2 + 1)` is a deliberate convenience that the vanishing of out-of-support binomials makes free.
prerequisites: the convention Nat.choose a b = 0 for b > a

title: The Mirror Form From Mathlib's Antidiagonal Sum
content: Mathlib already proves the Fibonacci sum over the antidiagonal: `Nat.fib_succ_eq_sum_choose` gives $F_{n+1} = \sum_{p \in \mathrm{antidiagonal}\,n} \binom{p_1}{p_2}$, where the antidiagonal of $n$ is the set of pairs $(k, n-k)$. Rewriting it through `Finset.Nat.sum_antidiagonal_eq_sum_range_succ` converts that pair-indexed sum into a plain range sum, yielding the *mirror form* $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{k}{n-k} = F_{n+1}$ in a single `rw`. This is the load-bearing step: all the mathematics is already in the library; the work is choosing the right index presentation.

title: The Diagonal Form by Index Reflection
content: The two index conventions $\binom{k}{n-k}$ and $\binom{n-j}{j}$ are related by the single reflection $j \mapsto n - j$. The proof rewrites by the mirror form and `Finset.sum_range_reflect`, which sends $\sum_{k} f(k) = \sum_{j} f(n-j)$ over `range (n+1)`. What remains is pure natural-number subtraction bookkeeping: under the range bound $j \le n$, the two equalities $n+1-1-j = n-j$ and $n-(n-j) = j$ — each closed instantly by `omega` — line the reflected summand up termwise with $\binom{n-j}{j}$. `omega` is exactly the right tool here because truncated $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction makes these identities false without the hypothesis $j \le n$.
